tagline: A dirt loop around Chimney Peak, where the Pacific Crest crosses.
intro: The byway leaves Route 178 at Canebrake and heads north on Canebrake Road, graded dirt, into a rugged stretch of the southern Sierra Nevada. About nine miles up it reaches a junction, circles Chimney Peak, 7,871 feet, and comes back to Canebrake Road at Lamont Meadow.

Wilderness lies on both hands: the Domelands on the left going up, Owens Peak on the right, and Chimney Peak on the left past the junction. The old Sacatar Trail, a wagon road into the Owens Valley once used by soldiers and cattlemen, crosses the Chimney Peak Wilderness.

moments.title: Canebrake
moments.text: Canebrake Creek was named in 1853 for the sugary reeds Indians were gathering there. In Prohibition the area kept a speakeasy and a still, run by a bootlegger named Victor Hugo.

moments.title: Chimney Creek Campground
moments.text: The Pacific Crest Trail crosses the road just south of this campground, where 36 sites sit among pinyon pines, grey pines and oaks along Chimney Creek at 5,700 feet.

moments.title: Long Valley
moments.text: From the junction, Long Valley Road leads to a two-mile spur and a primitive campground, where the unmaintained Volpe Trail runs three miles to the South Fork of the Kern River.

practical: Canebrake Road is graded dirt. The two-mile Long Valley campground road typically requires a high-clearance 4x4.
